notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Health is more than the absence of disease.
  • The World Health Organization describes health in terms of physical, mental and social well-being.
  • Good health depends on nutrition, hygiene, sanitation, safe water, exercise, sleep, environment and access to healthcare.
  • Disease prevention is generally more effective and less costly than treatment after severe illness develops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Health → Physical + Mental + Social Well-being

2. Hygiene
  • Hygiene refers to practices that help maintain health and prevent disease.
  • Personal hygiene reduces transmission of infectious organisms.
  • Community hygiene includes safe water, sanitation, waste disposal and environmental cleanliness.
  • Food hygiene prevents food-borne disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hygiene → Disease Prevention

3. Personal Hygiene

Important personal-hygiene practices include:

  • Regular handwashing.
  • Bathing.
  • Oral hygiene.
  • Wearing clean clothes.
  • Nail care.
  • Hair and scalp hygiene.
  • Safe menstrual hygiene.
  • Proper toilet practices.
  • Respiratory hygiene.
4. Handwashing
  • Hands are important vehicles for transmission of infectious organisms.
  • Washing with soap and water removes dirt, organic matter and many microbes.
  • Handwashing is especially important before eating or preparing food and after using the toilet.
  • It is also important after coughing, sneezing or handling waste.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Most Basic Infection-Prevention Practice → Handwashing

5. Handwashing with Soap
  • Soap helps remove oils, dirt and microorganisms from skin.
  • Mechanical rubbing and rinsing are important parts of cleaning.
  • Handwashing reduces faeco-oral transmission of many diseases.
6. Important Times to Wash Hands

Wash hands:

  • Before preparing food.
  • Before eating.
  • After toilet use.
  • After cleaning a child who has defecated.
  • After handling garbage.
  • After coughing or sneezing into the hands.
  • Before and after caring for a sick person when appropriate.
7. Alcohol-Based Hand Rub
  • Alcohol-based hand rub is useful when hands are not visibly dirty.
  • It rapidly reduces many microorganisms.
  • Soap and water are preferred when hands are visibly soiled.
  • Some infectious agents and chemical contaminants may require soap-and-water washing.
8. Respiratory Hygiene
  • Coughing or sneezing can release respiratory droplets.
  • Cover the mouth and nose with tissue or elbow rather than bare hands.
  • Dispose of used tissues safely.
  • Hand hygiene should follow contact with respiratory secretions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cough/Sneeze → Cover + Hand Hygiene

9. Bathing
  • Regular bathing removes sweat, dirt and microorganisms.
  • It helps maintain skin health.
  • Excessively harsh soaps or repeated aggressive washing can damage the skin barrier.
10. Skin
  • Skin is the largest organ of the human body.
  • It acts as the first physical barrier against many pathogens.
  • Intact skin reduces entry of microorganisms.
  • Cuts and wounds should be cleaned and protected.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Largest Human Organ → Skin

11. Nail Hygiene
  • Dirt and microorganisms can collect under fingernails.
  • Nails should be kept reasonably short and clean.
  • Nail biting can increase transfer of microbes from hands to mouth.
12. Hair and Scalp Hygiene
  • Regular washing removes excess oil, sweat and dirt.
  • Personal items such as combs should not be shared when there is risk of lice or fungal infection.
  • Head lice spread mainly through close head-to-head contact.
13. Oral Hygiene
  • Oral hygiene helps prevent dental caries and gum disease.
  • Teeth should be brushed regularly with fluoride-containing toothpaste where appropriate.
  • Cleaning between teeth helps remove plaque that brushing may miss.
  • Excess frequent sugar exposure increases dental-caries risk.
14. Dental Plaque
  • Dental plaque is a microbial biofilm that forms on teeth.
  • Plaque bacteria metabolise sugars and produce acids.
  • These acids can demineralise tooth enamel.
  • Persistent plaque near gums contributes to gingivitis.
15. Dental Caries
  • Dental caries is tooth decay caused by interaction of bacteria, fermentable carbohydrates and susceptible teeth over time.
  • Acid production lowers plaque pH.
  • Tooth enamel dissolution increases below a critical pH often cited around 5.5.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dental Caries → Bacteria + Sugar + Acid

16. Fluoride and Teeth
  • Fluoride helps make enamel more resistant to acid attack.
  • It supports remineralisation.
  • Excess fluoride during tooth development can cause dental fluorosis.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Adequate Fluoride → Caries Prevention

Excess Fluoride → Fluorosis

17. Gingivitis
  • Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums.
  • Plaque accumulation is a major cause.
  • Gums may become red, swollen and bleed easily.
  • Good oral hygiene can reverse many early cases.
18. Periodontitis
  • Untreated gum inflammation can progress to periodontitis.
  • Supporting tissues around teeth are damaged.
  • Severe disease can lead to tooth loosening and loss.
19. Menstrual Hygiene
  • Menstrual hygiene involves safe, clean and dignified management of menstruation.
  • Menstrual products should be changed at appropriate intervals.
  • Hands should be washed before and after changing products.
  • Reusable products should be properly washed and dried.
  • Menstruation is a normal physiological process, not a disease.
20. Menstrual Products

Common products include:

  • Sanitary pads.
  • Tampons.
  • Menstrual cups.
  • Reusable cloth pads.
  • Safe use depends on proper hygiene and correct product handling.
21. Menstrual Hygiene and Infection
  • Poor hygiene can increase skin irritation and local infection risk.
  • Menstrual materials should be stored clean and dry.
  • Used disposable products should be discarded safely.
22. Sleep
  • Sleep is essential for physical and mental health.
  • It supports memory, hormonal regulation, immunity and recovery.
  • Chronic sleep deprivation impairs attention, mood and metabolic health.
  • Sleep requirements vary by age.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sleep → Recovery + Memory + Hormonal Regulation

23. Exercise
  • Regular physical activity supports cardiovascular health.
  • It improves muscle and bone strength.
  • It helps maintain healthy body weight.
  • It improves insulin sensitivity and mental well-being.
  • Excessive inactivity is a risk factor for chronic disease.
24. Sedentary Behaviour
  • Sedentary behaviour involves prolonged low-energy sitting or reclining.
  • Long periods of inactivity are associated with higher risk of obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
  • Regular movement is important even for people who exercise.
25. Mental Hygiene
  • Mental hygiene refers to practices that support emotional and psychological well-being.
  • Adequate sleep, social support, stress management and physical activity contribute to mental health.
  • Persistent severe symptoms require appropriate professional assessment.
26. Stress
  • Stress is the body's response to physical or psychological demands.
  • Short-term stress can be adaptive.
  • Chronic uncontrolled stress can affect sleep, blood pressure, immunity and mental health.
27. Safe Drinking Water
  • Safe drinking water should be free from harmful pathogens and dangerous chemical contamination.
  • Water-borne diseases commonly spread when water is contaminated with human or animal faeces.
  • Safe water supply is a major public-health measure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Safe Water → Prevents Water-Borne Disease

28. Water-Borne Diseases

Important examples include:

  • Cholera.
  • Typhoid.
  • Hepatitis A.
  • Hepatitis E.
  • Poliomyelitis through faeco-oral transmission.
  • Several diarrhoeal diseases.
29. Cholera
  • Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae.
  • It spreads mainly through contaminated food and water.
  • It can cause profuse watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration.
  • Safe water, sanitation and ORS are key preventive and treatment measures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cholera → Vibrio cholerae → Contaminated Water

30. Typhoid
  • Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi.
  • It spreads through contaminated food and water.
  • Good sanitation and hand hygiene reduce transmission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Typhoid → Salmonella Typhi

31. Boiling Water
  • Boiling can kill most disease-causing microorganisms.
  • It does not remove dissolved salts, heavy metals or many chemical pollutants.
  • Therefore, boiling makes microbiologically unsafe water safer but does not solve every type of contamination.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Boiling → Kills microbes

Boiling ≠ Removes all chemicals

32. Filtration
  • Filtration removes suspended particles.
  • Appropriate filters can also remove many microorganisms.
  • Effectiveness depends on filter type.
  • Simple cloth filtration does not make all contaminated water completely safe.
33. Chlorination
  • Chlorine is widely used to disinfect drinking water.
  • It kills many disease-causing microorganisms.
  • Correct concentration and contact time are necessary.
  • Excessive chlorine is undesirable, while insufficient chlorine may fail to disinfect adequately.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Water Disinfection → Chlorination

34. Ozonation
  • Ozone is a powerful oxidising disinfectant.
  • It can destroy many microorganisms.
  • Unlike chlorine, it leaves little persistent disinfectant residual in distribution systems.
35. Ultraviolet Disinfection
  • UV radiation can inactivate microorganisms by damaging nucleic acids.
  • UV treatment does not remove dissolved chemical contamination.
  • Water clarity affects effectiveness.
36. Sanitation
  • Sanitation refers to safe management of human excreta, wastewater and environmental waste.
  • Proper sanitation prevents faeco-oral transmission.
  • Toilets should prevent contamination of water sources and living areas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sanitation → Safe Excreta and Waste Management

37. Open Defecation
  • Open defecation contaminates soil and water.
  • Flies and other vectors can transfer faecal organisms to food.
  • It increases risk of diarrhoeal disease and parasitic infection.
  • Safe toilet use is a major public-health intervention.
38. Faeco-Oral Route

The faeco-oral route can involve:

  • Contaminated water.
  • Contaminated food.
  • Dirty hands.
  • Flies.
  • Contaminated utensils and surfaces.
📌 Memory

Faeces → Fingers/Flies/Food/Fluids → Mouth

39. Food Hygiene

Food hygiene includes:

  • Safe cooking.
  • Safe storage.
  • Clean utensils.
  • Handwashing.
  • Separation of raw and cooked foods.
  • Protection from insects and rodents.
  • Safe water use.
40. Cross-Contamination
  • Cross-contamination is transfer of harmful microorganisms from one food or surface to another.
  • Raw meat can contaminate cooked food.
  • Separate cutting boards and utensils reduce risk.
  • Hands should be washed after handling raw animal foods.
41. Cooking
  • Adequate cooking kills many pathogenic microorganisms.
  • Food should be heated thoroughly, especially meat, eggs and leftovers.
  • Cooking cannot reliably remove all toxins already produced by some microorganisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cooking may kill bacteria but may not destroy every preformed toxin.

42. Refrigeration
  • Refrigeration slows microbial growth.
  • It does not sterilise food.
  • Some microorganisms can still grow slowly at refrigerator temperatures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Refrigeration → Slows Growth, Does Not Sterilise

43. Freezing
  • Freezing greatly slows microbial growth.
  • Many microorganisms survive freezing.
  • Once food thaws, growth can resume.
44. Pasteurisation
  • Pasteurisation is controlled heat treatment used to reduce harmful microorganisms.
  • It is widely used for milk.
  • Pasteurisation does not completely sterilise food.
  • Louis Pasteur is associated with the underlying process.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pasteurisation → Reduces Pathogens, Not Sterilisation

45. Food-Borne Disease
  • Food-borne disease results from consuming contaminated food or drink.
  • Causes include bacteria, viruses, parasites and toxins.
  • Common symptoms include diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain and fever.
46. Food Poisoning
  • Food poisoning can result from infection or ingestion of toxins.
  • Staphylococcus aureus can produce heat-stable enterotoxins.
  • Botulism results from botulinum toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum.
47. Botulism
  • Botulism is caused by botulinum neurotoxin.
  • Clostridium botulinum is an anaerobic spore-forming bacterium.
  • Improperly canned foods are a classic risk.
  • The toxin can cause descending flaccid paralysis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Botulism → Clostridium botulinum

48. Food Preservation

Common methods include:

  • Refrigeration.
  • Freezing.
  • Drying.
  • Salting.
  • Sugaring.
  • Pickling.
  • Fermentation.
  • Canning.
  • Pasteurisation.
49. Waste Management

Waste can be classified broadly as:

  • Biodegradable.
  • Non-biodegradable.
  • Biomedical.
  • Hazardous.
  • Electronic waste.
50. Biodegradable Waste

Examples include:

  • Food waste.
  • Plant matter.
  • Paper in suitable conditions.
  • Animal waste.
  • Microorganisms can decompose biodegradable waste.
51. Non-Biodegradable Waste

Examples include:

  • Many plastics.
  • Glass.
  • Metals.
  • These persist for long periods if not recycled or safely managed.
52. 3R Principle

The classic waste-management hierarchy includes:

  • Reduce.
  • Reuse.
  • Recycle.
📌 Must-Memorise

3R → Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

53. Waste Hierarchy

A broader preferred sequence is:

  • Prevent/reduce.
  • Reuse.
  • Recycle.
  • Recover.
  • Dispose safely.
54. Composting
  • Composting converts biodegradable organic waste into nutrient-rich material.
  • Microorganisms decompose the waste.
  • Compost improves soil organic matter.
55. Vermicomposting
  • Vermicomposting uses earthworms and microorganisms.
  • It converts organic waste into useful manure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vermicompost → Earthworms

56. Biomedical Waste
  • Biomedical waste arises from healthcare activities.
  • It may contain infectious materials, sharps, pharmaceuticals or contaminated items.
  • It requires segregation and specialised treatment.
  • Improper disposal can spread infections and cause injuries.
57. Sharps
  • Needles, blades and other sharps can transmit blood-borne infections if reused or handled unsafely.
  • They require puncture-resistant disposal containers.
  • Reuse of disposable needles is unsafe.
58. Electronic Waste
  • E-waste includes discarded electronic equipment.
  • It may contain lead, mercury, cadmium and other hazardous substances.
  • Safe recycling prevents environmental contamination.
59. Vector
  • A vector is an organism that transmits a pathogen between hosts.
  • Mosquitoes, ticks, fleas and some flies act as disease vectors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vector → Disease Carrier

60. Mosquito-Borne Diseases

Important examples:

  • Malaria.
  • Dengue.
  • Chikungunya.
  • Japanese encephalitis.
  • Lymphatic filariasis.
61. Malaria Vector
  • Malaria is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Plasmodium is the causative parasite.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malaria → Plasmodium → Female Anopheles

62. Dengue Vector
  • Dengue is caused by dengue virus.
  • It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti.
  • Aedes mosquitoes commonly bite during daytime.
  • They breed in small collections of standing water.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dengue → Aedes aegypti

63. Chikungunya
  • Chikungunya is caused by chikungunya virus.
  • Aedes mosquitoes are important vectors.
  • Severe joint pain is a characteristic symptom.
64. Filariasis
  • Lymphatic filariasis is caused mainly by filarial worms such as Wuchereria bancrofti.
  • Mosquitoes transmit the infection.
  • Chronic disease can cause lymphatic swelling and elephantiasis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Filariasis → Wuchereria

65. Mosquito Control

Important measures include:

  • Remove stagnant water.
  • Cover water-storage containers.
  • Use mosquito nets.
  • Use window screens.
  • Use approved repellents.
  • Apply larval or adult vector control when required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Best Household Mosquito Prevention → Eliminate Breeding Water

66. Housefly
  • Houseflies can mechanically transfer pathogens.
  • They can carry faecal microorganisms from waste to food.
  • Proper waste disposal and food covering reduce risk.
67. Vaccination
  • Vaccination stimulates acquired immunity against specific diseases.
  • Vaccines expose the immune system to safe forms or components of a pathogen or its antigens.
  • Vaccination prepares immune memory without requiring natural disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vaccination → Artificial Active Immunity

68. Active Immunity
  • Active immunity develops when a person's own immune system responds to an antigen.
  • It occurs after infection or vaccination.
  • It usually develops more slowly but can provide long-lasting immune memory.
69. Passive Immunity
  • Passive immunity results from receiving ready-made antibodies.
  • Protection is immediate but generally temporary.
  • Maternal antibodies transferred to a baby are natural passive immunity.
  • Immunoglobulin injections provide artificial passive immunity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Passive Immunity → Ready-Made Antibodies

70. Natural Active Immunity
  • Natural active immunity develops following infection and immune response.
  • The duration varies greatly by disease.
71. Artificial Active Immunity
  • Artificial active immunity results from vaccination.
  • The body itself produces antibodies and memory cells.
72. Natural Passive Immunity

Examples:

  • Maternal IgG through placenta.
  • IgA through breast milk.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Colostrum → Passive Immunity through IgA

73. Artificial Passive Immunity

Examples include administration of:

  • Rabies immunoglobulin.
  • Tetanus immunoglobulin.
  • Antivenom.
  • These contain ready-made antibodies.
74. Vaccine Types

Broad vaccine types include:

  • Live attenuated.
  • Inactivated.
  • Toxoid.
  • Subunit/conjugate.
  • Recombinant.
  • Viral-vector.
  • Nucleic-acid vaccines.
75. Live Attenuated Vaccine
  • Contains a weakened form of the pathogen.
  • Usually produces strong immune responses.
  • Examples traditionally include BCG, measles, mumps and rubella vaccines.
76. Inactivated Vaccine
  • Contains killed/inactivated pathogen.
  • It cannot replicate.
  • Booster doses may be required.
  • Inactivated polio vaccine is an example.
77. Toxoid Vaccine
  • Toxoid vaccines contain inactivated bacterial toxins.
  • They protect against toxin-mediated disease.
  • Tetanus and diphtheria vaccines use toxoids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tetanus + Diphtheria → Toxoid Vaccines

78. BCG
  • BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin.
  • It is a vaccine against tuberculosis.
  • It is derived from attenuated Mycobacterium bovis.
  • It is particularly useful in protecting children against severe forms of TB.
📌 Must-Memorise

BCG → Tuberculosis

79. Polio Vaccines

Two major types are:

  • OPV → Oral Polio Vaccine.
  • IPV → Inactivated Polio Vaccine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

OPV → Oral

IPV → Inactivated Injection

80. MMR
  • MMR vaccine protects against:
  • Measles.
  • Mumps.
  • Rubella.
📌 Must-Memorise

MMR → Measles + Mumps + Rubella

81. DPT
  • DPT refers traditionally to protection against:
  • Diphtheria.
  • Pertussis.
  • Tetanus.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPT → Diphtheria + Pertussis + Tetanus

82. Herd Immunity
  • Herd immunity occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune, reducing transmission.
  • It indirectly protects some susceptible individuals.
  • Required immune proportion varies by disease.
  • Herd immunity does not mean every person is immune.
83. Antibiotics
  • Antibiotics act against bacteria.
  • They do not treat ordinary viral infections such as influenza.
  • Misuse promotes antibiotic resistance.
  • A full prescribed course should be followed according to medical advice.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Antibiotics → Bacteria

Not ordinary viruses

84. Antibiotic Resistance
  • Resistant bacteria survive antibiotic exposure.
  • They multiply and spread.
  • Unnecessary antibiotic use accelerates selection of resistance.
  • Antibiotics should not be used for viral colds without bacterial indication.
85. Antiseptic
  • Antiseptics are antimicrobial substances applied to living tissues.
  • They reduce microbial load.
  • Examples include some iodine and chlorhexidine preparations.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Antiseptic → Living Tissue

86. Disinfectant
  • Disinfectants are generally used on non-living surfaces.
  • They reduce or destroy microorganisms.
  • Many disinfectants are too harsh for direct use on living tissue.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Antiseptic → Living tissue

Disinfectant → Non-living surface

87. Sterilisation
  • Sterilisation destroys or removes all forms of microbial life, including bacterial spores.
  • It is stronger than routine disinfection.
88. Autoclave
  • Autoclave sterilises using steam under pressure.
  • A commonly cited condition is around 121°C under pressure for a specified period.
  • It is widely used for heat-resistant medical and laboratory equipment.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Autoclave → Steam under Pressure

89. Disinfection vs Sterilisation
  • Disinfection reduces or destroys many pathogenic microorganisms.
  • Sterilisation eliminates all viable microorganisms including spores.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Sterilisation > Disinfection in microbial elimination.

90. Quarantine
  • Quarantine restricts movement of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease but are not necessarily ill.
  • It helps prevent possible spread during the incubation period.
91. Isolation
  • Isolation separates people known or suspected to be infected from others.
  • It reduces transmission.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Quarantine → Exposed

Isolation → Infected/Suspected Infected

92. Incubation Period
  • Incubation period is the time between infection and appearance of symptoms.
  • It varies among diseases.
  • A person may sometimes transmit infection before symptoms appear.
93. Endemic
  • Endemic means a disease is consistently present in a particular population or geographic area.
94. Epidemic
  • Epidemic is occurrence of disease cases above the normally expected level in a community or region.
95. Pandemic
  • Pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across multiple countries or continents and affects many people.
📌 Must-Memorise

Endemic → Constant/local

Epidemic → Excess regional spread

Pandemic → International/global spread

96. Zoonosis
  • A zoonosis is an infection naturally transmitted between animals and humans.
  • Rabies is a classic zoonotic disease.
  • Some influenza viruses and several emerging infections have animal origins.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zoonosis → Animal ↔ Human Infection

97. Rabies
  • Rabies is caused by rabies virus.
  • It is usually transmitted through saliva from bites of infected mammals, especially dogs in many countries.
  • Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost invariably fatal.
  • Immediate wound washing and timely post-exposure vaccination are critical.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rabies → Virus → Animal Bite

98. Rabies First Aid
  • Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water.
  • Seek medical care urgently.
  • Post-exposure vaccination may be required.
  • Rabies immunoglobulin may be indicated for certain exposures.
99. Tetanus
  • Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani.
  • The bacterium produces a powerful neurotoxin.
  • Spores can enter through contaminated wounds.
  • Tetanus does not spread directly from person to person.
  • Vaccination prevents disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tetanus → Clostridium tetani → Toxin

100. First Aid — Wounds
  • Control bleeding with direct pressure.
  • Clean minor wounds with safe water.
  • Cover with clean dressing.
  • Deep, contaminated or animal-bite wounds require medical assessment.
  • Tetanus protection should be reviewed.
101. First Aid — Burns
  • Cool a fresh thermal burn with cool running water.
  • Do not apply ice directly to significant burns.
  • Do not break blisters deliberately.
  • Severe or extensive burns require urgent medical care.
102. First Aid — Fracture
  • Keep the injured part as still as possible.
  • Avoid unnecessary movement.
  • Support the limb if safe to do so.
  • Seek medical care.
103. First Aid — Fainting
  • Lay the person flat when appropriate.
  • Ensure adequate ventilation.
  • Loosen tight clothing.
  • Persistent unconsciousness or associated injury requires urgent medical evaluation.
104. Clean Environment
  • Environmental cleanliness reduces breeding sites for vectors.
  • Proper drainage prevents stagnant water.
  • Covered waste bins reduce flies and rodents.
  • Clean public spaces help prevent disease transmission.
105. Air Hygiene
  • Indoor air quality affects respiratory health.
  • Tobacco smoke, biomass smoke, mould and poor ventilation can harm health.
  • Adequate ventilation reduces concentration of indoor pollutants and some airborne pathogens.
106. Tobacco
  • Tobacco smoke contains nicotine, carbon monoxide and many carcinogenic chemicals.
  • Smoking increases risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease and chronic lung disease.
  • Passive smoking also harms non-smokers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Tobacco → Major Preventable Health Risk

107. Alcohol and Health
  • Excessive alcohol use can damage liver, brain, heart and other organs.
  • It increases accident risk.
  • Alcohol dependence is a health disorder requiring appropriate care.
108. Personal Cleanliness and Parasites
  • Wearing footwear reduces exposure to some soil-transmitted parasites.
  • Proper disposal of faeces reduces transmission of intestinal worms.
  • Washing vegetables reduces soil contamination.
  • Deworming programmes may be used in high-risk populations.
109. Hookworm
  • Hookworm larvae can penetrate skin from contaminated soil.
  • Wearing footwear reduces exposure.
  • Hookworm infection can contribute to iron-deficiency anaemia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hookworm → Skin Penetration + Anaemia

110. Ascariasis
  • Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides.
  • Infection follows ingestion of eggs from faecally contaminated soil, food or hands.
  • Sanitation and hand hygiene reduce transmission.
111. Pinworm Hygiene
  • Pinworm spreads through ingestion of microscopic eggs.
  • Handwashing and laundering bedding/clothing help interrupt transmission.
  • Reinfection within households is common.
112. Safe Food Storage
  • Cooked foods should be protected from flies and dust.
  • Perishable foods should not remain for long periods at warm temperatures.
  • Refrigeration slows microbial growth.
  • Leftovers should be reheated appropriately.
113. Clean Milk
  • Milk can support rapid bacterial growth.
  • Pasteurisation improves microbiological safety.
  • Boiling may further reduce microbial contamination in household settings.
114. Personal Utensils
  • Sharing razors, needles or toothbrushes can transmit blood or body-fluid-associated infections.
  • Needles must never be shared.
115. Blood-Borne Infections

Important blood-borne infections include:

  • HIV.
  • Hepatitis B.
  • Hepatitis C.
  • Transmission can occur through contaminated needles or blood exposure.
116. HIV
  • HIV stands for Human Immunodeficiency Virus.
  • It attacks cells of the immune system, especially CD4 T lymphocytes.
  • Untreated infection can progress to AIDS.
  • HIV is not spread by casual contact such as handshakes or sharing ordinary social space.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

HIV → CD4 T Cells

117. AIDS
  • AIDS stands for Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.
  • It represents advanced HIV infection with severe immune suppression and/or specific illnesses.
  • Antiretroviral therapy can greatly suppress HIV replication.
118. HIV Transmission

Major routes include:

  • Unprotected sexual exposure.
  • Contaminated blood.
  • Shared needles.
  • Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

HIV does not spread through mosquitoes.

119. Hepatitis B
  • Hepatitis B virus infects the liver.
  • It spreads through blood and body fluids.
  • A vaccine is available.
  • Chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hepatitis B → Vaccine Available

120. Hepatitis C
  • Hepatitis C virus mainly spreads through blood.
  • No vaccine is currently used for hepatitis C.
  • Modern antiviral medicines can cure most infections.
121. Safe Injection Practice
  • Sterile single-use needles prevent blood-borne disease transmission.
  • Needles should never be shared.
  • Used sharps require safe disposal.
122. Sexual Hygiene and Health
  • Barrier protection such as condoms reduces transmission risk for many sexually transmitted infections.
  • Testing and early treatment help prevent complications.
  • Some STIs can be asymptomatic.
123. STI

STI stands for Sexually Transmitted Infection.

Examples include:

  • HIV infection.
  • Syphilis.
  • Gonorrhoea.
  • Chlamydia.
  • Genital herpes.
  • HPV infection.
  • Hepatitis B.
124. Syphilis
  • Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum.
  • It is a bacterial STI.
  • Untreated infection progresses through multiple stages.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

125. Gonorrhoea
  • Gonorrhoea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • It is a bacterial STI.
  • Untreated infection can cause reproductive complications.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gonorrhoea → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

126. HPV
  • HPV stands for Human Papillomavirus.
  • Some HPV types cause genital warts.
  • High-risk types are linked to cervical and other cancers.
  • HPV vaccination helps prevent infections caused by important cancer-associated types.
127. Cervical-Cancer Prevention

Important measures include:

  • HPV vaccination.
  • Cervical screening.
  • Early treatment of precancerous lesions.
  • Safer sexual practices.
128. Clean Surroundings and Vector Control
  • Uncovered water containers favour Aedes breeding.
  • Blocked drains can favour mosquito breeding.
  • Garbage can attract flies and rodents.
  • Community sanitation directly influences disease burden.
129. Rodent Control
  • Rodents contaminate food and can transmit diseases.
  • Food should be stored in sealed containers.
  • Waste should be disposed of properly.
  • Entry points into houses and stores should be blocked.
130. One Health
  • One Health recognises that human health, animal health and environmental health are interconnected.
  • Zoonotic diseases and antimicrobial resistance are major One Health issues.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

One Health → Human + Animal + Environment

131. Public Health
  • Public health focuses on prevention of disease and promotion of health at population level.
  • Important areas include vaccination, sanitation, nutrition, surveillance and health education.
132. Epidemiology
  • Epidemiology is the study of distribution and determinants of health-related events in populations.
  • It helps identify causes, risk factors and patterns of disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Epidemiology → Disease Patterns in Populations

133. Incidence
  • Incidence refers to new cases occurring in a population during a specified period.
134. Prevalence
  • Prevalence refers to all existing cases in a population at a particular time or over a period.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Incidence → New Cases

Prevalence → Existing Cases

135. Mortality
  • Mortality refers to death in a population.
  • Mortality rate measures deaths relative to population size over time.
136. Morbidity
  • Morbidity refers to illness or disease within a population.
  • It is different from mortality.
137. Screening
  • Screening tests apparently healthy people for possible disease or risk.
  • Screening does not itself always establish a final diagnosis.
  • Positive screening results often require confirmatory testing.
138. Health Education
  • Health education promotes informed behaviours.
  • It improves hygiene, nutrition, vaccination uptake and disease prevention.
  • Community participation is important for sustained public-health improvement.
139. Clean Water and Diarrhoea Prevention

Most important measures include:

  • Safe drinking water.
  • Sanitary toilets.
  • Handwashing with soap.
  • Safe disposal of children's faeces.
  • Safe food preparation.
  • Breastfeeding and appropriate infant feeding.
140. ORS in Diarrhoea
  • ORS stands for Oral Rehydration Solution.
  • It replaces water and electrolytes lost in diarrhoea.
  • It does not directly kill the infectious organism.
  • Continued feeding and appropriate medical evaluation are important.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

ORS → Treats dehydration, not the pathogen itself.

141. Zinc in Childhood Diarrhoea
  • Zinc supplementation is commonly used in management of acute childhood diarrhoea under public-health protocols.
  • It can reduce duration and severity in many children.
142. Healthy Lifestyle

A healthy lifestyle generally includes:

  • Balanced diet.
  • Regular physical activity.
  • Adequate sleep.
  • Avoiding tobacco.
  • Limiting harmful alcohol use.
  • Maintaining hygiene.
  • Preventive healthcare.
143. Non-Communicable Diseases

Major NCDs include:

  • Cardiovascular diseases.
  • Cancer.
  • Diabetes.
  • Chronic respiratory diseases.
  • Many share behavioural and metabolic risk factors.
144. Major Modifiable NCD Risk Factors
  • Tobacco use.
  • Unhealthy diet.
  • Physical inactivity.
  • Harmful alcohol use.
  • Obesity.
  • High blood pressure.
145. Communicable Disease
  • Communicable diseases are caused by infectious agents capable of transmission directly or indirectly.
  • Bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths can cause communicable diseases.
146. Non-Communicable Disease
  • Non-communicable diseases are not transmitted from person to person as infections.
  • Examples include diabetes, hypertension and most cancers.
147. Hygiene and Immunity
  • Hygiene reduces pathogen exposure but does not replace normal immune development.
  • Excessive fear of all microbes is unnecessary because many microorganisms are harmless or beneficial.
  • The goal is safe hygiene, not complete sterility of everyday life.
148. TNPSC Scientist/Concept Links
  • Louis Pasteur → Pasteurisation and germ theory contributions.
  • Edward Jenner → Smallpox vaccination.
  • Robert Koch → Germ-disease links and Koch's postulates.
  • Joseph Lister → Antiseptic surgery.
  • John Snow → Cholera epidemiology.
  • Walter Cannon → Homeostasis.
149. Edward Jenner
  • Edward Jenner pioneered smallpox vaccination.
  • He used cowpox material to protect against smallpox.
  • His famous vaccination experiment was performed in 1796.
📌 Must-Memorise

Edward Jenner → Smallpox Vaccine → 1796

150. Joseph Lister
  • Joseph Lister promoted antiseptic surgical techniques.
  • He used carbolic acid/phenol in nineteenth-century surgery.
  • His work greatly reduced surgical infections.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joseph Lister → Antiseptic Surgery

151. John Snow
  • John Snow investigated the 1854 cholera outbreak in London.
  • He linked cases to contaminated water from the Broad Street pump.
  • He is often called a pioneer of modern epidemiology.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

John Snow → Cholera → Epidemiology

152. Robert Koch
  • Robert Koch demonstrated specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.
  • He developed Koch's postulates.
  • He identified the bacterium causing tuberculosis.
  • He also worked on cholera.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Robert Koch → Germ Theory Evidence + Koch's Postulates

153. Must-Memorise Hygiene–Disease Links
  • Unsafe water → Cholera/Typhoid.
  • Stagnant water → Mosquito breeding.
  • Dirty hands → Faeco-oral disease.
  • Shared needles → Blood-borne infections.
  • Poor oral hygiene → Dental caries/Gum disease.
  • Open defecation → Faecal contamination.
  • Excess fluoride → Fluorosis.
  • Poor ventilation → Indoor-air problems.
154. Must-Memorise Vector Pairs
  • Malaria → Female Anopheles.
  • Dengue → Aedes.
  • Chikungunya → Aedes.
  • Filariasis → Mosquito vector.
  • Plague → Fleas associated with infected rodents in classic transmission cycles.
155. Must-Memorise Immunity Pairs
  • Vaccination → Active immunity.
  • Immunoglobulin injection → Passive immunity.
  • Placental IgG → Natural passive immunity.
  • Colostrum IgA → Natural passive immunity.
  • Antivenom → Artificial passive immunity.
156. Must-Memorise Hygiene Instruments/Processes
  • Autoclave → Steam sterilisation.
  • Pasteurisation → Controlled heat reduction of pathogens.
  • Chlorination → Water disinfection.
  • ORS → Rehydration.
  • Vaccine → Preventive immunity.
  • PPE → Exposure reduction.
157. TNPSC Traps
  • Health is more than absence of disease.
  • Hygiene means disease-prevention practices.
  • Handwashing interrupts faeco-oral transmission.
  • Boiling kills many pathogens but does not remove all chemical contaminants.
  • Chlorination disinfects water.
  • Pasteurisation is not sterilisation.
  • Refrigeration slows microbes but does not sterilise food.
  • Cross-contamination can move microbes from raw to cooked food.
  • Open defecation promotes faecal contamination.
  • Malaria vector → Female Anopheles.
  • Dengue vector → Aedes aegypti.
  • Aedes commonly breeds in small stagnant-water collections.
  • Vaccination produces active immunity.
  • Immunoglobulin provides passive immunity.
  • BCG protects against tuberculosis.
  • DPT → Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus.
  • MMR → Measles, Mumps, Rubella.
  • Antibiotics do not treat ordinary viral infections.
  • Antiseptics are used on living tissues.
  • Disinfectants are used mainly on non-living surfaces.
  • Sterilisation destroys spores; ordinary disinfection may not.
  • Quarantine and isolation are different.
  • Quarantine → Exposed.
  • Isolation → Infected.
  • Endemic, epidemic and pandemic are different.
  • Rabies is viral.
  • Tetanus is bacterial and toxin-mediated.
  • HIV does not spread through mosquito bites.
  • Hepatitis B has a vaccine.
  • Hepatitis C has no routine vaccine.
  • HPV vaccination helps prevent cervical cancer.
  • ORS treats dehydration, not the infectious cause.
  • Incidence means new cases.
  • Prevalence means all existing cases.
  • 3R → Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
  • Biomedical sharps require safe disposal.
  • E-waste may contain toxic metals.
  • One Health links humans, animals and environment.
158. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Health → Physical + mental + social.
  • Hygiene → Prevention.
  • Hands → Soap.
  • Water → Boil/chlorinate.
  • Sanitation → Safe excreta.
  • Food → Cook + separate + store.
  • Pasteurisation → Not sterilisation.
  • Malaria → Anopheles.
  • Dengue → Aedes.
  • Cholera → Vibrio.
  • Typhoid → Salmonella Typhi.
  • Vaccine → Active immunity.
  • Antibody injection → Passive.
  • BCG → TB.
  • DPT → Diphtheria/Pertussis/Tetanus.
  • MMR → Measles/Mumps/Rubella.
  • Antibiotic → Bacteria.
  • Antiseptic → Living tissue.
  • Disinfectant → Surface.
  • Autoclave → Steam pressure.
  • Quarantine → Exposed.
  • Isolation → Infected.
  • Rabies → Virus.
  • Tetanus → C. tetani.
  • HIV → CD4 cells.
  • 3R → Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
  • Incidence → New.
  • Prevalence → Existing.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is health? → State of physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease.
  • What is hygiene? → Practices that maintain health and prevent disease.
  • Most basic personal infection-prevention practice? → Handwashing with soap.
  • Why is soap useful? → Removes dirt, oils and microorganisms from skin.
  • When is handwashing especially important? → Before food preparation/eating and after toilet use.
  • Largest human organ? → Skin.
  • Dental plaque is? → Microbial biofilm on teeth.
  • Dental caries develops mainly due to? → Bacterial acid production from sugars.
  • Critical enamel pH commonly cited? → Around 5.5.
  • Adequate fluoride helps prevent? → Dental caries.
  • Excess fluoride causes? → Fluorosis.
  • Safe drinking water should be free from? → Pathogenic microbes and harmful chemical contamination.
  • Water-borne disease example? → Cholera.
  • Causative organism of cholera? → Vibrio cholerae.
  • Typhoid organism? → Salmonella Typhi.
  • Does boiling remove all dissolved chemicals? → No.
  • Common drinking-water disinfectant? → Chlorine.
  • Open defecation causes? → Faecal contamination of soil and water.
  • Faeco-oral disease spreads through? → Contaminated hands, water and food.
  • What is cross-contamination? → Transfer of harmful microbes between foods/surfaces.
  • Does refrigeration sterilise food? → No.
  • Does freezing necessarily kill all microorganisms? → No.
  • Pasteurisation does what? → Reduces harmful microorganisms by controlled heating.
  • Pasteurisation equals sterilisation? → No.
  • Food poisoning from improperly canned food can be caused by? → Clostridium botulinum.
  • Botulism toxin affects mainly? → Nervous system.
  • 3R means? → Reduce, Reuse, Recycle.
  • Vermicomposting uses? → Earthworms.
  • Biomedical sharps should be discarded in? → Puncture-resistant containers.
  • Vector means? → Organism transmitting a pathogen.
  • Malaria vector? → Female Anopheles mosquito.
  • Malaria parasite? → Plasmodium.
  • Dengue vector? → Aedes aegypti.
  • Aedes mosquitoes commonly bite when? → Mainly during daytime.
  • Best household mosquito prevention? → Eliminate stagnant breeding water.
  • Filariasis parasite commonly asked? → Wuchereria bancrofti.
  • What does vaccination produce? → Artificial active immunity.
  • Active immunity means? → Body produces its own immune response.
  • Passive immunity means? → Ready-made antibodies received.
  • Antibodies crossing placenta represent? → Natural passive immunity.
  • Colostrum provides mainly which passive antibody? → IgA.
  • Antivenom is? → Artificial passive immunity.
  • BCG vaccine protects against? → Tuberculosis.
  • BCG full form? → Bacillus Calmette-Guérin.
  • DPT protects against? → Diphtheria, pertussis and tetanus.
  • MMR protects against? → Measles, mumps and rubella.
  • OPV stands for? → Oral Polio Vaccine.
  • IPV stands for? → Inactivated Polio Vaccine.
  • Toxoid-vaccine examples? → Tetanus and diphtheria.
  • Herd immunity means? → Population immunity reduces transmission and indirectly protects susceptible people.
  • Do antibiotics treat influenza? → No.
  • Antibiotics mainly act against? → Bacteria.
  • Major danger of unnecessary antibiotic use? → Antibiotic resistance.
  • Antiseptic used on? → Living tissue.
  • Disinfectant used on? → Non-living surfaces.
  • Sterilisation means? → Elimination of all viable microorganisms including spores.
  • Autoclave uses? → Steam under pressure.
  • Common autoclave temperature cited? → About 121°C.
  • Quarantine applies mainly to? → Exposed people who may develop disease.
  • Isolation applies mainly to? → Infected or suspected infected people.
  • Incubation period means? → Time from infection to symptoms.
  • Endemic means? → Disease consistently present in an area.
  • Epidemic means? → Cases above expected level in a region.
  • Pandemic means? → Epidemic spread across countries/continents.
  • Zoonosis means? → Infection transmitted between animals and humans.
  • Rabies causative agent? → Rabies virus.
  • Important first aid after suspected rabid-animal bite? → Immediate thorough washing and urgent medical care.
  • Tetanus causative organism? → Clostridium tetani.
  • Does tetanus spread directly person to person? → No.
  • HIV full form? → Human Immunodeficiency Virus.
  • Major target cells of HIV? → CD4 T lymphocytes.
  • AIDS full form? → Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.
  • Does HIV spread through mosquitoes? → No.
  • Hepatitis B vaccine available? → Yes.
  • Hepatitis C vaccine available? → No routine vaccine.
  • Syphilis organism? → Treponema pallidum.
  • Gonorrhoea organism? → Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • Virus associated with cervical cancer? → High-risk HPV.
  • Important cervical-cancer prevention? → HPV vaccination and screening.
  • Hookworm can enter body through? → Skin from contaminated soil.
  • Hookworm infection may contribute to? → Iron-deficiency anaemia.
  • Ascaris infection route? → Ingestion of eggs from faecal contamination.
  • What is One Health? → Integrated human, animal and environmental health approach.
  • Study of disease distribution in populations? → Epidemiology.
  • Incidence means? → New cases.
  • Prevalence means? → Existing cases.
  • Morbidity means? → Illness.
  • Mortality means? → Death.
  • ORS full form? → Oral Rehydration Solution.
  • Main purpose of ORS? → Replace lost water and electrolytes.
  • Does ORS kill diarrhoeal pathogens? → No.
  • Scientist associated with smallpox vaccination? → Edward Jenner.
  • Year of Jenner's famous vaccination experiment? → 1796.
  • Scientist associated with antiseptic surgery? → Joseph Lister.
  • Scientist associated with Broad Street cholera investigation? → John Snow.
  • Scientist associated with Koch's postulates? → Robert Koch.
  • Core TNPSC memory line? → Handwashing → prevention; Safe water + sanitation → diarrhoea control; Malaria → Anopheles; Dengue → Aedes; Vaccine → active immunity; Antibody → passive immunity; Autoclave → sterilisation; Incidence → new cases; Prevalence → existing cases.
